history.heading: Indus Valley and Vedic India
paragraphs: The Indus Valley Civilisation, with cities such as Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira, flourished from around 2600 to 1900 BCE across present-day Pakistan and northwest India, with advanced urban planning and drainage. Later, the Vedic period saw the composition of the Vedas, the foundations of Hinduism, in Sanskrit.
In the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, the Buddha and Mahavira, founders of Buddhism and Jainism, taught in the Ganges plain.

history.heading: Great empires
paragraphs: The Maurya Empire unified most of the subcontinent in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE; Emperor Ashoka converted to Buddhism and spread its message. The Gupta Empire (4th–6th centuries CE) is considered a golden age of science, mathematics and art; Indian mathematicians developed the decimal system and the concept of zero. In the south, dynasties such as the Cholas built great temples and maritime trade networks.

From the 12th century, Muslim dynasties ruled the north through the Delhi Sultanate. The Mughal Empire, founded by Babur in 1526, reached its height under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal.

history.heading: British rule
paragraphs: The British East India Company gained control of Bengal after 1757 and expanded across India. After the 1857 uprising, the British Crown took direct control, ruling the British Raj. Colonial rule brought railways and English education but also deindustrialisation and devastating famines.

The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, led the independence movement. Mahatma Gandhi pioneered non-violent mass resistance, including the 1930 Salt March, alongside leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel and B. R. Ambedkar.

history.heading: Independent India
paragraphs: India became independent on 15 August 1947, but the subcontinent was partitioned into India and Pakistan, causing mass migration of around 15 million people and communal violence that killed hundreds of thousands to a million or more. Gandhi was assassinated in 1948. India adopted its constitution in 1950, becoming a republic.

Nehru led India until 1964, pursuing non-alignment and state-led development. India fought wars with Pakistan and China. Indira Gandhi imposed a state of emergency from 1975 to 1977. Economic liberalisation from 1991 brought rapid growth. Since 2014 the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) under Narendra Modi has governed.

culture.heading: Diversity
paragraphs: India is the world's most populous country and one of the most diverse. Hindi and English are used for central government, and the constitution recognises 22 scheduled languages, including Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Tamil, Urdu and Gujarati, with hundreds more spoken.

About 80 percent of Indians are Hindu, and India has one of the world's largest Muslim populations, as well as Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Jains. Festivals such as Diwali, Holi, Eid, Durga Puja and Pongal are widely celebrated.

culture.heading: Arts and cinema
paragraphs: India has ancient traditions of classical music (Hindustani and Carnatic), dance (Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Odissi and others), sculpture and architecture. Literature ranges from the epics Mahabharata and Ramayana to Rabindranath Tagore, the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature, and modern writers.
India produces more films than any other country; Bollywood in Mumbai and film industries in Tamil, Telugu and other languages are hugely popular. Yoga originated in India.

culture.heading: Food and cricket
paragraphs: Indian cuisine varies enormously by region, from the wheat-based dishes and curries of the north to rice, dosa and coconut-based dishes in the south. Spices are central, and vegetarianism is widespread.

Cricket is a national obsession, and the Indian Premier League is one of the richest sports leagues in the world. India won the Cricket World Cup in 1983 and 2011 and the T20 World Cup in 2007 and 2024.

politics.heading: The world's largest democracy
paragraphs: India is a federal parliamentary republic of 28 states and 8 union territories. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the Lok Sabha (lower house), whose members are elected in the world's largest elections, with nearly a billion eligible voters. The president is head of state.

The BJP, a Hindu nationalist party, has dominated national politics since 2014; in the 2024 election it lost its outright majority but continued to govern with coalition partners. The Indian National Congress leads the opposition. Critics have raised concerns about pressure on press freedom, minorities and opposition.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: India pursues "strategic autonomy", maintaining ties with the United States, Russia and others. It is a member of the G20, BRICS and the Quad. Relations with Pakistan are tense, especially over Kashmir; in May 2025 the two countries exchanged military strikes. India also has a border dispute with China, which led to deadly clashes in 2020.

economy.heading: A rising economy
paragraphs: India has one of the world's largest and fastest-growing major economies. Services, especially information technology, software and business process outsourcing, centred on cities such as Bangalore and Hyderabad, are a major strength. Manufacturing is growing, including pharmaceuticals (India is called the "pharmacy of the world"), cars, electronics and smartphones.

Agriculture still employs a large share of the workforce. India's digital public infrastructure, including the UPI instant payment system and the Aadhaar identity system, is widely admired. The currency is the rupee.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: India has lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, but poverty and inequality remain significant. Challenges include creating jobs for a young, growing workforce, low female labour force participation, infrastructure gaps, air pollution, water stress and climate change.
